title: Phase-sensitive cascade quantum amplifier with nearly noiseless operation
authors: Ilari Lilja, Ekaterina Mukhanova, Michael Perelshtein, Kirill Petrovnin, Stanislav Khaldeev, Visa Vesterinen, Gheorghe Sorin Paraoanu, Pertti Hakonen
abstract: Phase-sensitive parametric devices enable quadrature-selective amplification with the potential for sub-quantum-limited noise performance. In this work, we investigate the operation of a SQUID-based Josephson Parametric Amplifier (JPA), comparing its performance in the phase-preserving and phase-sensitive regimes. The device, fabricated using VTT SWAPS technology, is driven in a three-wave mixing configuration and characterized in a reflection-based measurement setup at millikelvin temperatures. To directly probe the noise performance at low JPA gains, we employ a cascaded amplification scheme in which a Traveling-Wave Parametric Amplifier (TWPA) provides low-noise pre-amplification of the JPA output. In a phase-preserving operation, the JPA exhibits near-quantum-limited performance with a system noise temperature of $351\pm53$ mK at 6 GHz. In contrast, phase-sensitive operation yields a minimum system noise temperature of $94\pm12$ mK, well below the standard quantum limit of 288 mK. Our results demonstrate that a JPA-TWPA amplifier cascade opens the door to direct, high-fidelity probing of quantum devices without the need for background noise subtraction.
summary: The authors report on a superconducting quantum amplifier cascade (JPA-TWPA) designed for ultra-low-noise microwave measurements. By operating the Josephson Parametric Amplifier in a phase-sensitive regime, they achieved a system noise temperature significantly below the standard quantum limit. This technique enables direct, high-fidelity probing of quantum devices without complex background noise subtraction.
main_problem: The research investigates phase-sensitive quantum amplification using superconducting circuits to achieve noise performance below the standard quantum limit.
main_result: Phase-sensitive operation in a JPA-TWPA cascade achieved a minimum system noise temperature of $94 \pm 12$ mK, significantly beating the standard quantum limit of 288 mK.
method: The performance was characterized by comparing noise added in phase-preserving versus phase-sensitive parametric amplification regimes using a cascaded amplifier setup.
model_or_system: The core system is a Josephson Parametric Amplifier (JPA) based on a SQUID, which is cascaded with a Traveling-Wave Parametric Amplifier (TWPA). The device is fabricated using VTT SWAPS technology and operated at millikelvin temperatures.
key_observables: System noise temperature ($T_S$), added noise temperature ($T_N$), and output quadrature variances ($\Delta X^2_{	ext{out}}$, $\Delta P^2_{	ext{out}}$).
important_parameters: Operating frequency of 6 GHz; the standard quantum limit (SQL) of 288 mK; the phase-sensitive regime ($\omega_s = \omega_p/2$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the JPA being driven in a three-wave mixing configuration and utilizes the Friis formula for cascade noise estimation.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the device setup, comparing JPA performance in phase-preserving versus phase-sensitive modes, and plotting noise temperatures versus JPA gain.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the theoretical framework for noise analysis in parametric devices, compares the noise performance of phase-preserving versus phase-sensitive regimes, and presents experimental results demonstrating sub-SQL noise levels using the JPA-TWPA cascade.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant to quantum optics and open quantum systems as it demonstrates a practical method to measure quantum noise below the standard quantum limit using superconducting circuits.

figures.caption: Fig. 1 a) Schematic of the sample and the low-temperature configuration of the experimental setup. For studies of phase-sensitive amplification, a TWPA is added to the output side of the JPA, where it acts as a pre-amplifier, with a circulator and a directional coupler/diplexer in between. This is done to ensure that the strong pump tone can be applied at the input of the TWPA without affecting the operation of the JPA. b) An optical image of the sample with a close-up of the SQUID and its flux bias line (vertical strip). The JPA reflection port is seen at the top while the two pads at the bottom are for supplying flux bias and drive for the SQUID. Each pad is bonded using two Al wires.

Fig. 2 a) Phase-preserving parametric amplification as a function of signal frequency, showing the narrow-band performance of the JPA on top of the TWPA performance. b) The initial system noise temperature (at GJPA = 0 dB) of approximately TS,TWPA ≃0.75 K is achieved in part due to the pre- amplification provided by the TWPA. (Right side) c) Gain as a function of relative phase difference between signal and pump θ in the degenerate operating mode of the JPA. d) Phase dependence of TN in degenerate operation. When the signal and pump are out of phase, deamplification occurs, and the input-referred noise appears to increase as a result.

Figure 3 shows the JPA added noise temperature, TN,JPA, and the corresponding system noise temperature, TS,JPA, as functions of JPA gain. In the phase-preserving regime, the added noise increases with gain and saturates at 200±54 mK, correspond- ing to approximately 56 mK above the standard quantum limit of Tq = ℏωs/(2kB) = 144 mK. In contrast, during phase-sensitive operation the added noise saturates at only 17 ± 12 mK, well below the quantum limit for phase-preserving amplification. Expressed in terms of added input-referred noise, the phase-preserving mode adds 0.71 photons, whereas the phase-sensitive mode adds only 0.06 photons. Note tha approximately 6 dB enhancement in signal visibility is achieved in phase-sensitive operation. b) TN,JPA and c) TS,JPA as functions of GJPA. At very low gain, no noise is added to the measurement by the JPA, while at sufficiently large gains the added noise becomes nearly constant.
